column2: What would we ever do without our dependable microwave ovens?
If you've ever had to be without one at mealtime,
you realize how much we depend on it to make cooking faster and easier.
The microwave oven is one of the great inventions of the 20th century.
More than 90% of homes in America have at least one.
But do people always make sure food cooked in a microwave oven is safe before eating it?
Not always - especially when microwaving frozen convenience foods.
A couple of years ago, Salmonella bacteria in frozen convenience foods made quite a few people sick.
The problem was that a frozen chicken product was breaded and it looked fully cooked.
Some consumers didn't read the label that indicated these products should not be microwaved.
So they became sick a few hours after eating an undercooked product.
For foods labeled safe to be cooked in the microwave,
microwave ovens can cook food as well as other cooking appliances do.
But how do you know when the microwaved food has reached a safe temperature?
The same way you can test food cooked using ovens, stoves, outdoor grills and small appliances
-by using a food thermometer.
But that's the last step in getting food from microwave to table safely. Let's step back and see what should come first.
It's very easy: Read the package directions and do what they recommend.
If a range of times listed on the package says 3 to 5 minutes,
it's because some microwave ovens have a higher wattage than others.
Higher wattage ovens would take 3 minutes, and lower wattage ovens could take 5 minutes.
If you don't know the wattage of your microwave oven, watch to the videocast titled "Microwave Wattage."
It's always best to microwave the product for the shortest time given.
If it hasn't reached a safe temperature, you can always add more time.
But if you overcook and ruin the food, you can't take time away.
Microwave ovens can cook unevenly and leave "cold spots" in the food where harmful bacteria could survive.
Halfway through the cooking time, open the door and turn the dish so the food cooks more evenly.
The center is the last part of the food to reach a safe temperature.
Microwaves penetrate the food to a depth of 1 to 1½ inches.
In thicker pieces of food, the microwaves don't reach the center.
That area would cook by conduction of heat from the outer areas of the food into the middle.
When you think the food is hot enough, use a food thermometer and push the tip into the center of the food.
Test the temperature there and in several other places
to be sure it has reached the temperature given on the package throughout the product. Then eat and enjoy!
Want to reduce your risk of food poisoning? Go to www.foodsafety.gov
